items.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002
items.q: Vernon Alley and Eddie Alley, are two brothers here, they, along with Wesley Peoples, they formed a band.

ctx.x: I’m curious if your parents were — did they feel good about you pursuing music as a career?

Well it’s kind of tragic in a way. See my mother and father, they’re from Birmingham, Alabama. And my grandparents on his side, they own land, and they worked the land, and also from what I understand they would provide seed and fertilizer, and then the neighbors, they would all sharecrop and then they’d split the proceeds. And my dad, let’s see I had three aunts and two uncles, and so my dad, they sent him to an industrial school in Tennessee, which later I guess became part of the school system, the college…

that he went to Handy — W.C. Handy’s music store there in Nashville, Tennessee. Now my dad was born what, in the 1890s, so that had to be what, the early 1900s. He used to tell me that story. And my dad played ukulele and he sang and he would sing “Waiting for Ships that Never Come In” and they would do the recitations. Oh yeah. That’s when people would visit. Because the big thing then was visiting in various homes and entertaining. And my mother — on my father’s side my grandfather was a preacher. He was…
